decision: Shut down the legacy enterprise segment to put the whole team on the new self-serve product

framing.context: The legacy enterprise segment is $4.2M ARR, shrinking 6% per year, gross margin 71%, and it funds 100% of the company's operations — we have not raised since 2020 and have $900k in the bank. It requires 11 of our 34 people (support, implementation, two account managers). The new self-serve product has $210k ARR growing 22% month over month with 3 engineers on it. Two of our four largest enterprise accounts are also the design partners whose usage data trains the self-serve product's defaults. Winding down enterprise means 60-day contractual notice on renewals and the loss of roughly $3.4M of the next twelve months' cash.
options: Hard cut: sunset enterprise now, all 34 people on self-serve
Staged: freeze new enterprise sales, keep renewals and the two design-partner accounts, move 6 people per quarter to self-serve

members.name: CEO
members.decisive_reason: Half-pivots are how companies die slowly.

answers.P1_timing: Renewal notices go out 2023-09-30, so the decision forces itself.
answers.P2_reversibility: 1-way. Enterprise customers will not come back once sunset.
answers.P3_expected_value: Self-serve at 22% MoM reaches $4M ARR in about 15 months if the growth holds.
answers.P4_downside_cap: $900k in the bank against a $3.4M cash hole.
answers.P5_opportunity_cost: Every quarter split is a quarter the self-serve product ships slower.
answers.P6_information: Whether 22% MoM survives the first 10x of volume.
answers.P7_second_order: A clean story makes the next raise easier.
answers.P8_strategy_fit: Self-serve is the company we want to be.
answers.P10_kill_criteria: Self-serve growth under 10% MoM for two consecutive months.

members.name: CFO
members.decisive_reason: There is no version of this where $900k covers a $3.4M hole.

answers.P1_timing: The 60-day notice window is the only hard date.
answers.P2_reversibility: Cash is the most irreversible thing here.
answers.P3_expected_value: 22% MoM on $210k is a small base; it does not reach payroll in time.
answers.P5_opportunity_cost: Enterprise gross profit is the cheapest capital we will ever have.
answers.P6_information: What the self-serve CAC and churn look like at 10x volume.
answers.P7_second_order: Losing the two design-partner accounts removes the data that makes self-serve good.
answers.P8_strategy_fit: The destination is right; the funding plan is missing.

known_good.recommendation_class: MODIFY — staged wind-down, not a hard cut: freeze new enterprise sales, keep renewals and specifically retain the two design-partner accounts, and migrate people to self-serve in tranches funded by enterprise gross profit, with explicit kill criteria on self-serve growth
known_good.decisive_fact: The legacy segment is the pivot's only source of funding and its only source of training data. $900k in cash against a $3.4M twelve-month cash hole means a hard cut makes the company insolvent well before self-serve can reach payroll, and sunsetting the two design-partner accounts removes the usage data the new product's defaults depend on. The segment is not a distraction to be cut; it is the balance sheet and the data pipeline.
known_good.what_actually_happened: Hard cuts in this pattern ran out of cash mid-transition and were sold for less than the legacy ARR was worth. Staged wind-downs — freeze new sales, harvest renewals, migrate headcount in tranches — reached self-serve escape velocity with dilution-free funding.
known_good.why_it_was_right: The right answer preserves optionality and sequencing: the destination (self-serve) is correct, but the constraint is cash and data, so the decision is about pacing, not direction.
